---
title: "Predicting US Drug Shortages"
subtitle: "Can federal supply-side data warn us before a drug runs short?"
---

## The Problem

Drug shortages are a persistent feature of the US healthcare system. They affect everything from
over-the-counter medications to the sterile injectables used in surgery, chemotherapy, and
emergency care. When a shortage hits, hospitals substitute, ration, or delay treatment; pharmacies
scramble to source alternatives; and patients face interrupted therapy, higher prices, or care
that is simply postponed.

The operational problem is not only that shortages happen — it is that **warning time is
unpredictable**. A shortage may be announced weeks or months after supply has already tightened,
or a drug may quietly disappear with no announcement at all. Because the lead time is so
variable, stockpiling is both expensive and poorly targeted. Vizient estimates that managing
shortages costs US hospitals roughly **$900 million per year in labor expenses alone**
[@vizient2019], before counting price increases or the clinical cost of unavailable medication.

This project asks a practical question: **using only public federal data, can we tell in advance
which drugs are heading for shortage?**

## Who This Affects

| Stakeholder | Stake in the problem |
|---|---|
| **Patients** | Interrupted or substituted therapy, delayed procedures, higher out-of-pocket cost |
| **Hospitals & health systems** | Labor cost of mitigation, substitution protocols, rationing decisions |
| **Pharmacies** | Sourcing, inventory risk, patient communication |
| **Clinicians** | Forced therapeutic substitution, often with less-familiar alternatives |
| **Group purchasing organizations** | Contract and inventory planning across many facilities |
| **FDA and regulators** | Early detection, mitigation authority, supply-chain policy |

The most direct beneficiaries of better warning are hospital pharmacy directors and purchasing
groups, who currently make stockpiling decisions with little forward visibility.

## What Is Already Done — and What Is Missing

FDA maintains a public drug shortage list, and the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists
maintains a parallel set of shortage bulletins. FDA's own task force has analyzed root causes and
attributed most shortages to economic conditions in low-margin generic markets rather than to any
single manufacturing failure [@fda2019roots]. This infrastructure is fundamentally **reactive**:
it documents shortages once they are detected, which is useful for response but not for
anticipation.

Two structural gaps motivate this project.

**First, the historical record is actively destroyed.** FDA purges resolved shortages from its
public file after roughly six months. As of September 2026 the live file retained only **7
resolved records** out of 1,634. Counting shortage onsets from the live file yields just 3–17 per
year, and only for shortages that never resolved — a severely length-biased sample. Any attempt to
learn from that file alone is training on survivors.

**Second, supply-side withdrawal data is largely unused.** FDA's NSDE file retains product records
after they are delisted, which makes it possible to observe manufacturers exiting a product
*before* any shortage is declared. Existing public attempts at shortage prediction do not use it.

### Recovering the History

We reconstructed the shortage record from 102 Internet Archive captures of FDA's CDER shortage
file spanning 2019–2026. This recovers **10,967 shortage episodes across 1,416 drugs**, including
**2,028 with resolution dates** — versus 7 in the live file.

![Reconstructed drug-level shortage onsets per year, compared with what is visible in FDA's live shortage file. The live file retains only long-running, unresolved shortages, understating annual onsets by roughly an order of magnitude. Reconstructed from 102 Internet Archive captures of FDA's CDER shortage CSV. 2018 is left-censored (captures begin 2019-10-20) and 2026 is a partial year.](figures/shortage-onsets-by-year.png){#fig-onsets}

@fig-onsets is the central motivation for this project's data strategy: the gap between the two
series is the training data that a naive approach would silently discard.

## Project Blueprint

Over the semester the team plans to:

1. **Reconstruct shortage labels** from archived FDA files, recovering onset and resolution dates
   that the live file no longer carries.
2. **Build an analysis panel** at the active ingredient &times; route of administration level — 2,897
   approved prescription units — joined across product, approval, recall, and Medicare
   utilization data.
3. **Test for leading indicators**: whether package-level product delistings rise measurably
   before a shortage is declared, and with how much lead time.
4. **Evaluate predictability** under strict temporal validation — training on earlier years and
   testing on later ones — with a pre-registered list of banned leakage features.
5. **Report honestly on limits**, including where the reconstructed record is incomplete and how
   performance varies across periods with different dominant shortage causes.

The emphasis is on evidence about a real operational problem, not on comparing algorithms.
